title: Grattan Institute modelling found that limiting negative gearing and halving the capital gains discount would lower house prices by about 2 per cent
oneLiner: The most-cited independent estimate puts the price effect in the low single digits.
body: Grattan's 2016 analysis estimated that both reforms together would reduce prices by roughly 2 per cent and reduce the share of homes bought by investors, with little effect on rents. It is the figure most often quoted on both sides.
contextBackground: A single number does a lot of work in this debate. Supporters of reform cite it to show rents would not spike; opponents of reform cite the same number to show the price effect is too small to justify the change.
contextDisagreement: The estimate is accepted as a fair reading of the report. The argument is about what it implies, and whether a decade of further price growth has changed the magnitude.

evidenceItems.citation: Grattan Institute, Hot property: negative gearing and capital gains tax reform (2016), chapter 5

claimItself.title: Limiting negative gearing to new builds would make housing materially more affordable
claimItself.oneLiner: Removing the tax advantage for investors in existing homes would take heat out of the market first-home buyers compete in.
claimItself.body: Investors and first-home buyers bid for the same established dwellings. Removing a concession available only to one side would, proponents argue, shift enough demand to make a visible difference to prices and to who wins at auction.
